output.title: Place Value Detectives: Building and Breaking Numbers Through Thousands

objectives.text: Identify the value of each digit in a four-digit whole number (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) and state what each digit represents.
Read, write and represent whole numbers through thousands in standard form, word form and expanded form.
Compose and decompose four-digit numbers in more than one way (for example, 3,452 = 3,000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 34 hundreds + 5 tens + 2 ones).
Compare and order whole numbers through thousands using place-value reasoning and the symbols <, > and =.

activities.description: Warm-up number talk (whole class, carpet or front-of-room). Display the number 247 and ask: 'What is the 4 worth? What is the 2 worth? How many tens are hiding in this number?' Record student thinking on the board. Then reveal 2,047 and ask what changed and why the zero matters. Use quick hands-up responses and one pair-share so all 25 pupils engage within a few minutes.

Mini-lesson with place-value mats. Each pupil has a mat labelled Thousands | Hundreds | Tens | Ones and a set of digit cards 0-9. Model building 3,506 on the mat, then write it in three forms on the board: standard (3,506), word (three thousand, five hundred six), expanded (3,000 + 500 + 0 + 6). Explicitly name the zero as a placeholder. Pupils build two teacher-called numbers on their own mats and hold them up for a quick scan; circulate to check that digits sit in the correct columns.

Paired 'Number Detective' task. Each pair receives a set of four clue cards, for example: 'My number has 5 thousands, 2 more hundreds than thousands, 3 tens and 0 ones' or 'My number is 4,000 + 300 + 60 + 8.' Pairs build the number on the mat, write it in standard and expanded form, and record one sentence explaining how they know. Pairs then swap one card with a neighbouring pair and check each other's answers, ticking or fixing.

Compare and order quick-fire. Pairs receive four number cards (for example 4,208; 4,280; 4,028; 4,802) and order them from smallest to largest on a desk strip, inserting < or > between adjacent cards. Prompt: 'Which digit do you look at first, and why?' Take two or three pair explanations to the whole class, emphasising that we compare the thousands digit first, then move right.

Exit ticket and close. Pupils independently answer three items on a slip: (1) write 6,305 in expanded form; (2) state the value of the 7 in 2,741; (3) circle the greater number: 3,509 or 3,590. Collect slips at the door. Close with a 30-second recap where two pupils state one thing they learned about the thousands place.

differentiation.support: For pupils who need scaffolding, provide pre-printed place-value mats with column headings and colour coding (thousands blue, hundreds red, tens green, ones yellow), base-ten blocks or bundled straws for the thousands and hundreds, and clue cards that use only expanded form before moving to verbal clues. Reduce the paired task to two cards and allow numbers with no zero first. A support adult or confident peer can read clue cards aloud. Sentence starters are provided for the explanation ('I know this because the digit ___ is in the ___ column, so it is worth ___').
differentiation.extension: For pupils ready for challenge, pose open questions: 'Using the digits 3, 0, 7 and 5 once each, make the greatest and smallest four-digit numbers and explain your reasoning'; 'What number has 42 tens and 6 ones?'; 'Find two different ways to decompose 5,060.' Extension pupils can also create their own detective clue cards for a partner, including one deliberately tricky card with an internal zero, and write a comparison statement using < and > with two four-digit numbers that share the same thousands digit.

assessment.text: Exit-ticket slip with three items (expanded form of 6,305; value of the 7 in 2,741; comparing 3,509 and 3,590) to check each pupil's grasp of digit value, decomposition and comparison.
Observation during the paired Number Detective task: check that pupils place digits in the correct columns on the mat and can justify a digit's value in a spoken sentence.
Peer-check of swapped clue cards, where pairs tick or correct a neighbour's standard and expanded forms, giving a quick formative signal of accuracy across the class.

output.feedback: Give immediate, specific verbal feedback during circulation, naming the place-value idea rather than just right or wrong, for example: 'You put the 5 in the thousands column, so it is worth 5,000 — tell me what the 3 is worth.' Use the exit tickets to sort pupils into three quick groups for the next lesson: secure (move to rounding and comparing larger numbers), developing (revisit decomposition with internal zeros), and needing support (rebuild four-digit numbers with base-ten materials). Return exit slips at the start of the next lesson with one written comment each, such as 'Remember the zero holds the hundreds place' or 'Great expanded form — now try writing it in words.' Encourage pupils to self-check by reading their number aloud and asking, 'Does my expanded form add back to my standard form?'
output.reason: The plan targets outcome MA-3.1.1.1 on place value of whole numbers through thousands for a mixed-ability Grade 3 class of 25 in 45 minutes. It moves from a short number talk to explicit modelling with place-value mats, then paired clue-based practice, comparison work and an individual exit ticket, giving concrete-to-abstract progression and multiple checks for understanding. Differentiation through colour-coded mats, base-ten materials and reduced tasks supports pupils who need scaffolding, while open digit-arrangement problems extend confident pupils. output.title: Place Value of Whole Numbers Through Thousands

objectives.text: Identify the value of each digit in a whole number through thousands, recognising that a digit's position (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands) determines its value.
Read and write whole numbers through thousands in standard form and in expanded form, explaining the place value of each digit.
Use place-value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest ten and the nearest hundred.

activities.description: Warm-up and hook (whole class): Display a four-digit number such as 3,472 on the board. Ask pupils what each digit is 'worth'. Collect ideas on a place-value chart (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) and establish that the position of a digit tells us its value. Link back to prior work on place value of whole numbers through thousands.

Guided modelling: Model building 3,472 with base-ten blocks or place-value counters on the chart. Show how the same number is written in standard form and expanded form (3,000 + 400 + 70 + 2). Think aloud about the value of each digit, then invite pupils to build and expand a second number (e.g., 2,058) with a partner.

Paired practice: Give each pair a set of number cards (0-9). Pupils draw four cards, make the largest and smallest four-digit numbers they can, record both on a place-value chart, and write each in expanded form. Circulate and question: 'Which digit is in the hundreds place? What is its value?'

Rounding connection: Using a number line marked in tens and hundreds, model rounding a three- or four-digit number to the nearest ten and then to the nearest hundred. Pupils complete three examples in their books, identifying the two 'friendly' numbers the target sits between.

Plenary and exit check: Pupils write one four-digit number of their choice, state the value of the thousands digit, and round the number to the nearest hundred. Share two responses and address misconceptions about zero as a placeholder.

differentiation.support: Provide place-value charts with column headings and base-ten blocks for pupils who need concrete support. Begin with three-digit numbers before moving to four digits, and use sentence frames such as 'The digit ___ is in the ___ place, so it is worth ___.' Reduce the number of rounding examples to two and supply a pre-marked number line.
differentiation.extension: Challenge pupils to make the largest and smallest four-digit numbers using four given digits, then explain their reasoning. Ask them to create a four-digit number where the thousands digit is worth 6,000 and the tens digit is worth 30, and to round several four-digit numbers to the nearest ten and hundred, justifying each choice.

assessment.text: Exit ticket: pupils write a four-digit number, identify the value of a named digit, write the number in expanded form, and round it to the nearest hundred.
Observation during paired card activity: check that pupils correctly read and record four-digit numbers on the place-value chart and explain digit values.
Rounding check: pupils round three given numbers to the nearest ten and nearest hundred, showing the two neighbouring multiples.

output.feedback: Give immediate verbal feedback during circulation, naming the specific place-value skill observed (e.g., 'You correctly identified that the 4 in 3,472 is worth 400'). Use the exit ticket to sort pupils into three groups for the next lesson: secure with four-digit place value, needs support with zero as a placeholder, and ready for rounding challenges. Provide written comments that point to the next step rather than only marking right or wrong.
output.reason: The curriculum evidence in chunk moe-ma-g3-000 explicitly covers place value of whole numbers through thousands (MA-3.1.1.1) and rounding to the nearest ten and hundred (MA-3.1.4.1, MA-3.1.5.1), so the requested outcome is fully supported.
